writtenQuestions.q: Calculate the volume of concrete for a slab 8m × 6m × 150mm thick, minus a 1-metre radius circular hole.
writtenQuestions.answer:
Slab volume = 8 × 6 × 0.15 = 7.2 m³

Circular hole volume = π × r² × depth = π × 1² × 0.15 = 0.471 m³

Net concrete volume = 7.2 − 0.471 = 6.729 m³ ≈ 6.73 m³

writtenQuestions.q: A tool is shown. Outline a suitable use for this tool. (2 marks)
writtenQuestions.answer: The tool shown is a router. A suitable use for this tool is to create a rebate (a step-shaped recess) along the edge of a timber board for joint construction, such as a rebate joint used when making drawers or cabinets. Other suitable uses include: edge profiling (decorative shaping of timber edges), cutting grooves and housings in timber, flush/pattern cutting using a template, and mortising.

writtenQuestions.q: Describe TWO settings or adjustments that may be required before using the router shown. (3 marks)
writtenQuestions.answer:
Two settings or adjustments required before using a router are:

1. Depth of cut: The depth gauge on the router is adjusted to set how deeply the cutter will enter the timber. This determines the depth of the rebate, groove or profile being cut and must be set precisely before beginning the cut.

2. Width of cut: The side fence (parallel guide) position is adjusted to control the distance from the edge of the timber to the cutting position, determining the width of the cut. Other acceptable adjustments include: selecting the appropriate cutter profile/shape for the operation, and setting the spindle speed (RPM) to suit the material and cutter diameter being used.

writtenQuestions.q: Outline considerations when selecting an abrasive for use with electric sanders. (2 marks)
writtenQuestions.answer: When selecting an abrasive for an electric sander, key considerations include: the grit size — coarser grits (e.g. 40–80 grit) for initial material removal and fine grits (e.g. 180–240 grit) for final finishing; the material being sanded — hardwoods require different abrasives to softwoods; the abrasive type — silicon carbide, aluminium oxide or garnet each suit different materials and applications; and the backing type — paper, cloth or Velcro/hook-and-loop backing depending on the sander type and the required durability of the abrasive sheet.

writtenQuestions.q: Describe TWO indicators which show that a tool is not performing efficiently, or has a fault. (3 marks)
writtenQuestions.answer:
Two indicators that a tool is not performing efficiently or has a fault are:

1. Smoke or burning smell: If a power tool produces smoke or a burning smell during operation, this indicates the motor is overloading, overheating, or that there is an electrical fault. This is a serious safety indicator and the tool must be immediately switched off and removed from service.

2. Excessive vibration or unusual noise: A tool that vibrates more than normal, produces grinding noises, rattles or makes unfamiliar sounds indicates worn bearings, a loose or damaged component, or an unbalanced cutting tool. These symptoms indicate a fault that could lead to failure or injury. Other valid indicators include: slower operation than normal, poor results/finish quality, failure to start, blockages, or excessive heat.

writtenQuestions.q: Explain how builders can protect their tools and equipment from theft and damage on site. (5 marks)
writtenQuestions.answer:
Builders can implement a range of strategies to protect their tools and equipment from both theft and physical damage on site.

To prevent theft, builders should use secure, lockable storage such as purpose-built toolboxes, steel job site boxes or shipping containers with heavy-duty padlocks and hasp-and-staple fixings. A sign-in/sign-out register should be maintained so tool location is always known. The site perimeter should be secured with fencing, gates and padlocks to restrict unauthorised access, and security lighting and CCTV cameras installed to deter theft and provide evidence if items are stolen. High-value items such as laser levels and power tools should be engraved with identification numbers or asset tags.

To prevent damage, tools should be stored in dedicated racks or cases to prevent them from being knocked or dropped. Power tools must be stored away from moisture, dust and extreme temperatures that can damage electronics and motors. Tools should be returned to storage after each use rather than left lying on site where they can be driven over or stepped on. Protective covers and blade guards should always be in place during storage and transport.

writtenQuestions.q: List the type of information that can be found in a building specification. (2 marks)
writtenQuestions.answer: A building specification contains detailed written information that complements the drawings, including: the species and grade of timber to be used; brick type, mortar mix ratios and quality; the composition and strength of concrete in footings and slabs; paint colours, brands and number of coats; PC (Prime Cost) items such as hot water systems, tapware, baths, appliances and light fittings; floor and wall tile types and fixing methods; roofing material types and fixing requirements; and waterproofing membrane specifications.

writtenQuestions.q: Identify the meaning of the following symbols or abbreviations found on construction drawings: HW, RWP, and the horizontal sliding window symbol shown. (3 marks)
writtenQuestions.answer:
HW = Hot Water (refers to the hot water supply pipe or hot water service connection on plumbing/services drawings)
RWP = Rainwater Pipe (the vertical downpipe that carries rainwater from the roof gutters to the stormwater drainage system)
Horizontal sliding window symbol (two rectangles with arrows pointing toward each other) = a window where the sashes slide horizontally past each other to open

writtenQuestions.q: Describe the range of information that can be found on a floor plan. (4 marks)
writtenQuestions.answer: A floor plan provides a comprehensive range of information about the internal layout and dimensions of a building. It shows the overall building footprint and dimensions, including the layout and names of all rooms and spaces (bedrooms, kitchen, bathroom, living areas). Wall locations and thicknesses are shown, along with the positions of all doors (and their swing direction) and windows. Structural elements such as columns and loadbearing walls are identified. Fixed appliances and fixtures are shown including kitchens (sink, stove, dishwasher), bathrooms (bath, shower, toilet, vanity) and laundries. Staircase location and direction of travel (with step count) are indicated. Built-in joinery such as wardrobes, pantries and linen cupboards are shown. Some floor plans also indicate floor coverings, ceiling heights, roof outline and eaves overhang, and the locations of downpipes.

writtenQuestions.q: Describe the control measures that can be used to minimise soil erosion on a construction site. (5 marks)
writtenQuestions.answer:
Soil erosion on a construction site can be minimised through a combination of physical barriers, vegetation management and site management practices.

Sediment control fences (silt fences) made from geotextile fabric are installed along site boundaries and drainage lines to intercept sediment-laden runoff and trap soil particles before they leave the site. Similarly, silt socks (sediment-filled tubes) can be placed around stormwater drain inlets to prevent sediment from entering the drainage system.

Erosion control blankets or mats made from jute, coir or synthetic materials are laid over exposed soil surfaces and steep areas to stabilise the soil, protect it from raindrop impact and reduce surface runoff velocity.

Maintaining or establishing temporary vegetation (such as a cover crop or hydroseeding) on disturbed areas that will not be worked immediately helps bind soil with root systems and protect the surface from rain impact.

The site should be graded to direct stormwater runoff to designated detention areas or sediment basins where sediment can settle before water is discharged. Limiting the area of disturbed ground at any one time and establishing temporary site driveways using coarse gravel aggregate prevents vehicles from tracking mud onto public roads.

Vehicle wash bays at site exits and restricting vehicle access to designated areas further reduces sediment transport off-site.

writtenQuestions.q: Explain techniques that could be used to minimise the risk of harm to workers when manually handling materials. Support your answer with relevant workplace examples. (10 marks)
writtenQuestions.answer:
Manual handling is one of the leading causes of injury in the construction industry, with back injuries, muscle strains and crush injuries being the most common outcomes. A range of techniques can be employed to minimise harm.

Risk assessment and task planning are the foundation of safe manual handling. Before any lifting or carrying task, workers should assess the weight of the load, the distance to be moved, the working posture required, and the frequency of the task. For example, moving 20 kg cement bags across a site requires planning the route, identifying rest points and considering team lifting.

Mechanical aids significantly reduce the physical demands of manual handling. Trolleys, sackbarrows, pallet jacks, forklifts, hoists and materials lifts should be used whenever the load weight or distance makes manual carrying impractical or hazardous. A bricklayer using a brick trolley to move a pack of bricks rather than carrying individual loads eliminates repeated bending and lifting strain.

Correct manual lifting technique must be trained and consistently applied. Workers should adopt a wide, stable stance, keep the load close to the body, bend at the knees (not the waist), keep the back in a neutral (straight) position, look forward (neutral neck position), and lift smoothly using leg muscles. Twisting the torso while carrying a load is a major cause of back injury and must be avoided.

Team lifting should be employed for heavy or awkward loads that exceed safe single-person limits (typically 20–25 kg for repeated lifts). Communication between team members (agreed signals and commands) is essential. For example, two workers carrying a door frame must coordinate their movements to prevent unexpected weight transfers.

Ergonomic workplace design reduces the need for hazardous postures. Storing materials at waist height where possible, pre-positioning materials close to the installation point, and breaking large deliveries into smaller manageable loads minimises extreme bending, reaching and carrying distances.

Regular breaks and job rotation allow fatigued muscles to recover, significantly reducing the risk of cumulative strain injuries. PPE such as steel-capped boots and gloves also supports safe manual handling.

writtenQuestions.q: Explain a range of strategies that can be used to improve resource efficiency in the construction industry. (15 marks)
writtenQuestions.answer:
Resource efficiency in the construction industry refers to maximising the value obtained from all inputs — materials, labour, equipment, time and money — while minimising waste in all its forms.

Materials management is one of the most impactful strategies. Accurate calculation of material quantities using take-off schedules and material lists prevents over-ordering (which leads to waste and unnecessary cost) and under-ordering (which causes project delays). Designing structures to suit standard material sizes — for example, designing wall heights to equal full plasterboard sheet widths (3000 mm) — eliminates unnecessary cutting and the resulting off-cuts, reducing both material waste and the labour time spent cutting and disposing of waste.

Just-in-time delivery sequencing improves resource efficiency by arranging for materials to arrive on site only when they are needed for the next stage of construction. This reduces damage to materials stored on site, frees up workspace for productive activity, and minimises double-handling of materials.

Labour resource efficiency depends on correct trade sequencing and workforce planning. Using Gantt charts and construction programs ensures trades can access the site to perform their work without interference from preceding trades. Having the right number of workers for each stage — not too few (creating bottlenecks) or too many (causing congestion and under-utilisation) — maximises productivity.

Technology and modern construction methods improve efficiency. CAD/CAM design allows more precise planning, reducing errors and rework. Prefabricated components (manufactured off-site to precise dimensions) arrive ready to install, reducing on-site labour time, waste and weather delays.

Tool and equipment maintenance ensures that plant and tools operate at their designed efficiency. A poorly maintained concrete mixer, compressor or power tool uses more energy, produces inferior results and requires more time to complete a task.

Sustainable practices such as recycling construction waste (crushed concrete for fill, timber offcuts for formwork), using recycled materials where appropriate, and minimising packaging waste all contribute to material resource efficiency while reducing environmental impact.

Effective supervision, clear work instructions and appropriate training ensure workers understand the expected standard of work, reducing errors, rework and the waste of materials and time associated with correcting mistakes.

boxes.heading: What is WHS?
boxes.html:
• WHS (Work Health and Safety) is the laws, policies and procedures that protect workers, visitors and the public from harm in a workplace
  • Duty of care — every business and worker in construction has a legal obligation to take reasonable care to protect their own health and safety, and that of others who may be affected by what they do (or fail to do)
  • WHS is everyone's responsibility, not just management's — every worker shares responsibility for identifying hazards and working safely

boxes.heading: The cost of workplace injury
boxes.html:
• Human — pain, injury, disability, and in the worst cases death or permanent trauma to the worker and their family
  • Social — loss of income, strain on relationships, reduced quality of life, burden on the healthcare system
  • Economic — workers compensation payouts, lost productivity, increased insurance premiums, potential fines
  • Organisational — damage to a company's reputation, loss of clients/contracts, low staff morale, project delays

boxes.heading: Key WHS bodies
boxes.html:
• SafeWork NSW — the NSW regulator that enforces WHS law, investigates incidents, and issues improvement/prohibition notices
  • Safe Work Australia — the national body that develops WHS policy and model laws, which states then adopt or adapt
  • Local councils — enforce building and development regulations that intersect with site safety, e.g. hoarding and public safety
  • Unions and professional associations (e.g. CFMEU, HIA, MBA) — represent worker/industry interests and provide WHS advice and training

boxes.heading: Sources of WHS information
boxes.html:
• Internal — site inductions, toolbox talks, workplace policies and procedures, safety data sheets (SDS), supervisors
  • External — the SafeWork NSW website and codes of practice, Australian Standards, industry associations, legislation

boxes.heading: Acts, Regulations, Codes of Practice & Standards
boxes.html:
• Act — the primary law passed by parliament, e.g. the Work Health and Safety Act 2011 (NSW) — sets out broad legal obligations
  • Regulation — more detailed rules made under the Act, e.g. the Work Health and Safety Regulation 2017 (NSW) — specifies how obligations must be met
  • Code of practice — practical guidance on complying with the Act/Regulation for a specific area (e.g. site induction, first aid, manual handling, risk management, WHS consultation) — not legally binding by itself, but following one is strong evidence of compliance
  • Standard (Australian, industry or workplace) — a technical benchmark for materials, products or processes

boxes.heading: Who holds duties under the Act
boxes.html:
• PCBU (Person Conducting a Business or Undertaking) — the primary duty holder; must ensure health and safety so far as reasonably practicable
  • Officer — a person who makes or influences decisions affecting the business (e.g. a director) — must exercise due diligence
  • Worker — anyone who carries out work for a PCBU (employee, apprentice, contractor) — must take reasonable care for their own safety and follow reasonable instructions
  • Some tasks legally require a license, permit, ticket or certificate of competency before a worker may perform them, e.g. operating certain plant, working at heights, asbestos removal

boxes.heading: WHS consultation & participation
boxes.html:
• Consultation means genuinely involving workers in WHS decisions that affect them — required by law, not just good practice
  • Workers can provide input through formal and informal discussion, meetings, surveys, training, WHS audits and inspections
  • A Health and Safety Representative (HSR) can be elected to represent workers in WHS consultation
  • A workplace must establish a WHS committee when requested by a worker or HSR, or once the business employs 20 or more workers — whichever comes first

boxes.heading: Reporting WHS issues
boxes.html:
• Reporting can be formal or informal, written or verbal — but must always go to the appropriate person, e.g. supervisor, PCBU or HSR
  • It's every worker's responsibility to identify and report WHS issues, concerns and hazards — not just management's
  • Reports and records must be handled according to workplace policy and regulatory requirements
  • Unsafe work practices and breaches of health and safety should be reported immediately, even if no one was hurt — near misses are early warnings

boxes.heading: Hazard vs risk
boxes.html:
• A hazard is anything with the potential to cause harm — e.g. an unguarded saw blade, a wet floor, a loud generator
  • A risk is the likelihood that a hazard will actually cause harm, combined with how severe that harm would be — the same hazard can carry different risk depending on context (e.g. a wet floor in a fenced-off area is lower risk than the same wet floor on a busy walkway)
  • Risk assessment means identifying hazards, then judging likelihood × severity to decide what controls are needed

boxes.heading: Types of hazards on a construction site
boxes.html:
• Hazardous and non-hazardous materials
  • Human factors (fatigue, inexperience, distraction) affecting self, colleagues or others
  • Manual handling; tools, equipment, machinery and plant
  • Work environment and weather; work processes and practices
  • Specific high-risk situations: working alone, at heights, in confined spaces, in/around excavations, near traffic and water, and with compressed air, electricity or liquids under pressure

rows.label: Description
rows.html: Remove the hazard completely so it can no longer cause harm

rows.label: Construction example
rows.html: Redesigning a job so work is never performed at height

rows.label: Description
rows.html: Replace the hazard with something less hazardous

rows.label: Construction example
rows.html: Using battery-powered tools instead of 240V corded tools in a damp area

rows.label: Description
rows.html: Physically separate people from the hazard

rows.label: Construction example
rows.html: Roping off a crane's lift zone so no one can walk underneath a suspended load

rows.label: Description
rows.html: Modify equipment or the work environment to reduce exposure

rows.label: Construction example
rows.html: Local exhaust ventilation, dust extraction systems, machine guards fitted to power tools

rows.label: Description
rows.html: Change work practices through procedures, training, signage or scheduling

rows.label: Construction example
rows.html: Safe work method statements (SWMS), toolbox talks, job rotation, testing and tagging schedules

rows.label: Description
rows.html: Personal protective equipment — the last line of defence, relied on only when higher controls aren't practicable

rows.label: Construction example
rows.html: Safety glasses, hearing protection, hard hats, gloves

blocks.label: Reading hierarchy-of-control questions
blocks.html: NESA loves describing a real action and asking which level of the hierarchy it belongs to. The trap: most described actions sit lower in the hierarchy than they sound. Testing and tagging equipment, providing training and using a safe work method statement all feel proactive, but they're administrative controls, not engineering controls — they rely on people following a procedure rather than changing the physical hazard itself. Ask: does this action remove or reduce the hazard (elimination, substitution, isolation, engineering), or does it just change how people behave around an unchanged hazard (administrative, PPE)?
Safe work procedures, PPE selection, incidents and emergency response — including first aid, fire safety and reporting — are covered in the next Safety topic, Safe Work Practices & Emergencies.

revisionQuestions.q: A business has grown to 22 workers and still has no WHS committee. Is this compliant with the Work Health and Safety Act 2011? Explain.
revisionQuestions.a: No. Under the WHS Act, a workplace must establish a WHS committee once the business employs 20 or more workers (or earlier if requested by a worker or Health and Safety Representative). At 22 workers, the business is required to have a committee in place.

revisionQuestions.q: Explain the difference between a hazard and a risk, using a construction example.
revisionQuestions.a: A hazard is anything with the potential to cause harm — e.g. an open excavation. A risk is the likelihood that the hazard will cause harm, combined with how severe that harm would be — e.g. the risk of someone falling into that excavation is higher if it's unfenced next to a busy walkway than if it's isolated and clearly signed.

revisionQuestions.q: A worker is asked to use a step ladder near a live overhead power line. Identify the hazard, and propose a risk control that sits higher in the hierarchy than wearing insulated gloves.
revisionQuestions.a: The hazard is electrocution from contact with the live overhead line. Insulated gloves are only a PPE control, the lowest level. A higher-level control would be to isolate the work area from the line (e.g. an exclusion zone, or de-energising the line) or eliminate the risk entirely by rescheduling the task so no work occurs near the line while it is live.

revisionQuestions.q: What is the difference between an Act, a Regulation and a Code of Practice in the WHS legal framework?
revisionQuestions.a: An Act is the primary law passed by parliament (e.g. the Work Health and Safety Act 2011 (NSW)), setting out broad legal duties. A Regulation is made under the Act and sets out more detailed rules for meeting those duties (e.g. the Work Health and Safety Regulation 2017 (NSW)). A Code of Practice gives practical guidance on complying with the Act and Regulation for a specific area, such as manual handling or site induction — it isn't legally binding on its own, but following it is strong evidence a business met its duty.

revisionQuestions.q: Name three of the human, social, economic or organisational costs of a serious workplace injury.
revisionQuestions.a: Accept any three, e.g.: human — pain, disability or death; social — loss of income, strain on relationships; economic — workers compensation payouts, increased insurance premiums, fines; organisational — reputational damage, lost contracts, low staff morale, project delays.

revisionQuestions.q: A new apprentice notices a frayed extension lead but doesn't report it because “it's not my job.” Explain why this reasoning is incorrect under WHS consultation and participation requirements.
revisionQuestions.a: WHS is everyone's responsibility, not just management's or supervisors'. Every worker has a duty to identify and report hazards and WHS issues as soon as they notice them, regardless of role or seniority — reporting a frayed lead immediately (even if it later turns out to be minor) is exactly the kind of participation the WHS Act expects. Failing to report it leaves the hazard in place for the next person.

boxes.heading: Safe work procedures & documents
boxes.html:
• WHS induction training happens at three levels: general, work-activity-specific and site-specific
  • Safe work relies on a set of standard documents: job safety analysis (JSA), safe work method statement (SWMS), safety data sheet (SDS), standard operating procedures (SOP), and the site/project safety plan
  • A SWMS is legally mandatory for "high-risk construction work" — e.g. work at heights above 2 metres, work in or near a confined space, or demolition
  • Hazardous substances and dangerous goods must be correctly handled, labelled, transported, stored and disposed of according to their SDS

boxes.heading: PPE — selection, fit & maintenance
boxes.html:
• Correct fit matters as much as wearing PPE at all — poorly fitted PPE can create new hazards, e.g. loose clothing caught in moving machinery
  • Common PPE: eye protection, hearing protection, respirators/masks, gloves, head protection, footwear, high-vis clothing, sunscreen
  • PPE is selected based on the specific hazard and task — one type doesn't suit every job
  • PPE must be regularly inspected, maintained and correctly stored to remain effective

boxes.heading: Manual handling technique
boxes.html:
• Correct technique: wide stance for stability, look forward (neutral neck position), bend at the knees, and lift using the leg muscles — not the back or arms — keeping the load close to the body
  • Avoid bending, twisting and overreaching while carrying a load
  • Use mechanical aids (trolleys, pallet jacks, hoists) or team lifting for heavy or awkward loads rather than always lifting manually
  • Recommended weight limits and task rotation reduce cumulative strain from repetitious tasks

boxes.heading: Ergonomics & housekeeping
boxes.html:
• Ergonomics means designing the task/workspace to fit the worker — correct tool placement, sitting/standing posture, adjustable equipment and task rotation all reduce strain
  • Housekeeping covers clean-up procedures for the immediate work area and the whole site, and correct storage/disposal of waste
  • Good housekeeping is a WHS issue, not just tidiness — clutter, spills and stray materials are trip and injury hazards

boxes.heading: Working with electricity
boxes.html:
• All electrical equipment must be tested and tagged, showing a current inspection date — a missing or expired tag means the tool must be removed from service and reported to a supervisor immediately, never used "more carefully" instead
  • Leads and power boards should be placed and secured to avoid trip hazards, including overhead runs
  • A residual current device (RCD) continuously monitors current and trips the circuit within milliseconds if it detects a leakage to earth (such as through a person receiving a shock)
  • Always check for the location of existing site utilities (buried or overhead power lines) before starting work

boxes.heading: Tools, equipment & machinery checks
boxes.html:
• Pre-operational checks come before every task — confirm machine guards are fitted, look for damage, and check the tool is rated for the job
  • Faults must be reported verbally to the appropriate person, and recorded on a job card or maintenance log
  • Faulty or unsafe equipment should be tagged out (safety tags and lockout) so it cannot be used until repaired
  • Regular maintenance and correct storage extend a tool's working life and keep it safe to use

boxes.heading: Asbestos containing materials (ACM)
boxes.html:
• Asbestos was widely used in older building materials (e.g. fibro sheeting, some vinyl floor tiles, roofing) — its fibres, if disturbed, cause serious long-term respiratory illness, including mesothelioma
  • Workers must be able to recognise the types of ACM and their possible locations in older structures, especially before renovation or demolition
  • Handling and removal is governed by strict workplace policy and government legislation, including the asbestos management code of practice

boxes.heading: High-risk work situations
boxes.html:
• Working at heights, in confined spaces, near others, with compressed air, and with dangerous materials all require specific procedures beyond standard safe work practices
  • Entering a confined space always requires an entry permit as the first step — before any PPE is put on or atmospheric testing begins
  • High-risk activities like these are exactly the kind of work a SWMS is legally required for

rows.label: When to use it
rows.html: Clothing fires on a person — always the correct choice; never aim a chemical extinguisher at a person

rows.label: When to use it

rows.label: When to use it
rows.html: Always check the extinguisher's label and colour band before use — the wrong type can spread or worsen a fire

boxes.heading: Incidents, accidents & emergencies
boxes.html:
• An incident is any unplanned event; an accident is an incident that results in injury, illness or damage; an emergency is a serious, urgent situation requiring an immediate response
  • First aid is different from an emergency — first aid is for a manageable injury a trained person can treat on-site; an emergency requires evacuation, emergency services or specialist response
  • The very first step of the DRSABCD first aid action plan is to check for Danger — a responder must not become a second casualty
  • Common workplace injuries include cuts, sprains, burns, falls and manual-handling strains, each needing different basic first aid

boxes.heading: Responding to an emergency
boxes.html:
• Know the location and use of emergency signals, alarms, exits, and emergency contact numbers before an emergency happens, not during one
  • Follow the workplace's procedures for notification, evacuation and securing the workplace/building
  • Basic firefighting equipment includes the fire blanket, fire extinguishers (chosen by class/colour band) and fire hose reels — know their location, class and maintenance status
  • After any incident, accident or emergency, recording and reporting must follow workplace policy and regulatory requirements — even near misses should be reported

blocks.label: Fire and first-aid questions are answered from the label, not guesswork
blocks.html: NESA's fire and first-aid MC questions are almost always testable directly from the extinguisher's colour band or the DRSABCD sequence — Danger, Response, Send for help, Airway, Breathing, CPR, Defibrillation. The most common trap is picking the "most active-sounding" first step (e.g. check breathing, or call emergency services) instead of the actual first step, which is always checking for danger to the responder. The same logic applies to fires on a person: even the correct extinguisher class for the fuel should never be aimed at someone — only a fire blanket, because of the physical injury the discharge itself could cause.

WHS's legal framework, the risk control hierarchy and WHS consultation & participation are covered in the previous Safety topic, WHS & Risk Management. The next focus area, Skills in Construction, begins with Plans, Drawings & Specifications.

revisionQuestions.q: A worker on a residential renovation accidentally cuts through an old fibro sheet and notices dust in the air. What material might this be, and what should the worker do?
revisionQuestions.a: This could be an asbestos containing material (ACM) — fibro sheeting was widely used in older buildings, and its fibres are extremely hazardous if disturbed, causing serious long-term respiratory illness. The worker should stop work immediately, avoid disturbing the material further, and follow workplace policy and the asbestos management code of practice rather than continuing to cut it.

revisionQuestions.q: Explain why a fire blanket, not a fire extinguisher, is the correct choice when a worker's clothing catches fire.
revisionQuestions.a: A fire blanket smothers the fire by cutting off its oxygen supply and is safe to wrap around a person. Chemical fire extinguishers (dry powder, foam, CO₂) can cause serious injury if discharged directly at a person — CO₂ causes cryogenic burns from its extreme cold, and dry powder's discharge pressure and residue can injure someone at close range.

revisionQuestions.q: A power tool's test-and-tag label is missing. What is the correct action, and why is "use it more carefully" not an acceptable response?
revisionQuestions.a: The tool must be removed from service and reported to a supervisor immediately, so it can be inspected, tested and tagged by a competent person before use. "Using it more carefully" doesn't address the real issue — without a current tag there is no evidence the tool is electrically safe, and it may already have been identified as faulty.

revisionQuestions.q: A worker needs to move fifteen 25 kg bags of cement by hand. Describe the correct manual handling technique.
revisionQuestions.a: Use a wide stance for stability, look forward keeping the neck neutral, bend at the knees (not the back), and lift using the leg muscles, keeping the load close to the body and avoiding twisting. Given the number and weight of the bags, mechanical aids (e.g. a trolley or pallet jack) or team lifting should also be considered rather than lifting all fifteen manually.

revisionQuestions.q: What is the very first step a worker must complete before entering a confined space, and what does this step involve?
revisionQuestions.a: Obtaining a valid permit to enter — this must happen before any PPE is put on or entry attempted. The permit process includes atmospheric testing, a risk assessment, emergency procedures and authorisation by a competent person.

revisionQuestions.q: A worker discovers a colleague who has collapsed near a live power source. Using the first step of the DRSABCD action plan, explain what the worker should do first, and why.
revisionQuestions.a: The worker should first check for Danger — assessing whether it's safe to approach, e.g. by isolating the power source or keeping clear of it — before going near the collapsed colleague. Rushing in without checking for danger risks the responder becoming a second casualty, which worsens the situation rather than helping it.

boxes.heading: What's on a title panel
boxes.html:
• Every plan has a title panel (usually bottom-right) recording: architect/drafting company, client, contractor, drawing number, date/version (including amendments), north indicator, number of pages, scale, and site location/address
  • Always check the title panel first — it confirms you're reading the correct, current version of the right drawing before using any dimension on it

boxes.heading: Symbols & conventions
boxes.html:
• Standard symbols and abbreviations are used for: contours, datum, dimensions, direction, levels, material types, orientation (north), projection, scale, services (electricity, gas, plumbing) and the situation of structures on site
  • Symbols follow Australian Standards so any tradesperson can read a plan the same way, regardless of who drew it — e.g. HW = hot water, RWP = rainwater pipe

boxes.heading: Pictorial vs working drawings
boxes.html:
• Pictorial drawings (illustrations, concept drawings, sketches) give a 3D representation of a project — used in initial planning to communicate major features and help clients/workers visualise the finished result
  • Working drawings are the precise, dimensioned 2D plans used to actually construct the building

boxes.heading: Detail drawings
boxes.html:
• Detail drawings enlarge a specific part of the construction (e.g. a joint or connection) at a larger scale — commonly 1:20, 1:10 or 1:5 — so tolerances and assembly notes stay legible
  • They include notes on dimensions and adherence to standards that couldn't be shown clearly on a full sectional view

boxes.heading: Project documentation
boxes.html:
• Building/engagement contracts record: costing/itemised quote, inclusions, material and finish specifications, stage schedule and payment schedule
  • Environmental plans link to legislation and company policy, and set out requirements/controls for bush fire, coastal management, flood zones, protecting significant cultural/historical sites, rehabilitation and waste management/disposal

boxes.heading: Specifications
boxes.html:
• A specification is a written document describing construction and finishing that can't be shown on the drawings — e.g. concrete composition, timber species/grade, brick type, mortar quality, paint colours, and PC (prime cost) items like tapware, appliances and hot water systems
  • Specifications and drawings must always be read together — the drawing shows where, the specification shows what and how

boxes.heading: Reading scale drawings
boxes.html:
• A scale like 1:100 means every 1 unit on the drawing represents 100 of the same unit in reality
  • Larger-scale drawings (e.g. 1:10) are used for small, detailed elements so they stay legible; smaller-scale drawings (e.g. 1:200) are used for whole-site plans
  • Always convert to consistent units before calculating (e.g. metres on-site vs millimetres on the plan)

boxes.heading: Keeping plans current
boxes.html:
• Amendments and version currency must always be checked before using a plan — an out-of-date version can lead to costly on-site errors
  • Any inconsistency found between plans, drawings and specifications must be reported through the correct procedure, not silently resolved on-site

blocks.label: Scale questions are pure unit conversion
blocks.html: Scale-conversion questions are graded on getting the units and division direction right, not on complex maths. Convert everything to the same unit first (usually millimetres), then divide by the scale factor for a real-to-plan conversion (or multiply for plan-to-real). Always sanity-check your answer: a 1:100 plan of a 13.7 m wall should give an answer measured in tens of millimetres, not centimetres or metres — if your answer doesn't "look like" a small line on a page, you've likely divided the wrong way.
Taking your own measurements and performing construction calculations — area, volume, unit conversions and material quantities — are covered in the next topic, Measurements & Calculations.

revisionQuestions.q: A retaining wall measures 22.4 metres in real life and is drawn at a scale of 1:200. How long is the line on the plan?
revisionQuestions.a: 22.4 m = 22,400 mm. At 1:200, 22,400 mm ÷ 200 = 112 mm. The line on the plan is 112 mm long.

revisionQuestions.q: Which type of plan would you check to find the north point, boundary setbacks, and the location of stormwater and sewer connections? Explain why.
revisionQuestions.a: The site/block plan — it shows the building's position on its own block, including orientation (north point), boundary dimensions and setbacks, contour lines/datum, and utilities such as stormwater and sewer. This information isn't shown on a floor plan or elevation.

revisionQuestions.q: A drawing shows a joint detail at a scale of 1:5, while the overall floor plan is drawn at 1:100. Explain why the two drawings use different scales.
revisionQuestions.a: Detail drawings use a much larger scale (e.g. 1:5 or 1:10) so small elements like joints and connections stay legible and can show precise dimensions and assembly notes. A floor plan uses a smaller scale (e.g. 1:100) because it needs to fit an entire level of the building on one page — using a large scale for the whole floor plan would make the page impractically large.

revisionQuestions.q: A specification states the brick type, mortar quality and paint colours for a house. Why isn't this information included directly on the drawings instead?
revisionQuestions.a: Drawings are for showing dimensions, layout and positioning — adding this much written detail would clutter them and make them harder to read. A specification is a separate written document specifically for information that can't be clearly illustrated on the drawings, such as material grades, finishes and PC items — the drawing and specification are meant to be read together.

revisionQuestions.q: A builder is using a set of plans on-site but isn't sure if it's the most recent version. What should they check, and why does this matter?
revisionQuestions.a: They should check the title panel for the date/version and any recorded amendments. Using an outdated version can lead to the wrong dimensions, materials or design being built — an expensive and time-consuming mistake to fix once construction has already started.

revisionQuestions.q: Explain the difference between a pictorial drawing and a working drawing, and give a reason each is used.
revisionQuestions.a: A pictorial drawing (e.g. a 3D illustration or sketch) gives a three-dimensional representation of the project, used in initial planning to help clients and workers visualise the finished result. A working drawing (e.g. a floor plan or elevation) is a precise, dimensioned 2D plan used to actually construct the building — it's accurate enough to build from, which a pictorial drawing is not.

boxes.heading: Key terminology
boxes.html:
• Area, volume, perimeter and circumference measure different things — area is 2D surface (m²), volume is 3D space (m³), perimeter/circumference is the distance around a shape's edge (m)
  • Ratio compares quantities to each other (e.g. a 1:2:3 concrete mix); tolerance is the acceptable margin of error for a measurement; estimation is a reasoned approximation, not a guess
  • Waste minimisation means calculating quantities carefully so as little material as possible is over-ordered or wasted on-site

boxes.heading: Measuring equipment
boxes.html:
• Common equipment: digital devices (including laser measure), retractable tape measure, rule, scales, squares, and the trundle wheel (for long ground distances)
  • Each tool has a correct use and limitation — a laser measure is fast and accurate over long straight distances but needs a clear line of sight; a retractable tape measure is accurate to 1 mm when the end hook and lock button are used correctly
  • Select the tool appropriate to the task, and clean/maintain/store it correctly afterwards, same as any other tool

boxes.heading: Units of measurement
boxes.html:
• Length — millimetres (mm) and metres (m), including m² (area) and m³ (volume)
  • Mass — grams (g) and kilograms (kg); larger loads use tonnes (t)
  • Liquid volume — millilitres (mL) and litres (L)

boxes.heading: Converting between units
boxes.html:
• mm → m: divide by 1,000 (e.g. 330 mm ÷ 1,000 = 0.330 m); m → mm: multiply by 1,000
  • kg → t: divide by 1,000; t → kg: multiply by 1,000
  • g → kg and mL → L: divide by 1,000
  • Always double-check which direction you're converting — an answer 1,000× too big or small is the most common error here

boxes.heading: Why accuracy matters
boxes.html:
• Incorrect measurements and calculations affect the client, the workplace/company and the environment — wrong material orders cause delays, extra delivery costs and wasted material
  • Under-ordering delays the project while waiting for a second delivery; over-ordering wastes money and creates unnecessary waste to dispose of

boxes.heading: Taking a linear measurement correctly
boxes.html:
• Identify a clear start and end point, and read the correct units and scale
  • Use a retractable tape measure safely and correctly: hook the end securely, and use the lock button to hold the reading steady
  • Aim for accuracy to within 1 mm on a construction site

rows.label: Formula
rows.html: Checks a corner is a true right angle — measure 3 units along one side and 4 along the other; if the diagonal between those points is exactly 5 units, the corner is square

rows.label: Calculation
rows.html: Convert slab depth to metres: 120 mm ÷ 1,000

boxes.heading: Determining material quantities
boxes.html:
• Materials are supplied in different forms — packed, loose, or compacted — and this affects how much you need to order
  • Some materials have standard supply quantities, e.g. timber in 300 mm increments, sheet materials by m², fencing/piping by lineal metre (Lm)
  • Always estimate within industry and workplace tolerances — a small buffer for cutting waste and offcuts is normal, not sloppy

boxes.heading: Recording & communicating results
boxes.html:
• Measurements, calculations and material requirements should be recorded in an appropriate location or format — e.g. ground spray on-site, or a written/digital work plan, job card or sketch
  • Records must be concise, legible and accurate, using correct industry abbreviations, symbols and standards
  • Always confirm and check recorded figures against the actual drawings, plans and specifications before ordering or building

blocks.label: Show every step of a calculation
blocks.html: Multi-step construction calculations (area → volume → cost, or quantity → wastage → pallets) are marked on the working, not just the final number. Write out each step separately, including the unit conversion, and round consistently — usually rounding up for quantities you need to buy (you can't purchase half a pallet or 0.6 of a fence panel) and to the nearest cent for cost. A correct final answer with no working shown can lose marks even if it's right; clear, logical working showing an almost-correct answer will often score better.
Reading plans, drawings and specifications — the source of most of the dimensions used in these calculations — was covered in the previous topic. Next, in Tools of the Trade: Hand & Power Tools.

revisionQuestions.q: A garden bed is 2,450 mm long. Convert this to metres.
A concrete path is 15 m long, 0.9 m wide and 100 mm deep. Calculate the volume of concrete required in m³.
revisionQuestions.a: Convert depth to metres: 100 mm ÷ 1,000 = 0.1 m. Volume = 15 m × 0.9 m × 0.1 m = 1.35 m³.

revisionQuestions.q: Explain the 3:4:5 method and what it's used for on a construction site.
revisionQuestions.a: The 3:4:5 method checks whether a corner is a true right angle. Measure 3 units along one side of the corner and 4 units along the other; if the diagonal distance between those two points is exactly 5 units, the corner is square. It's commonly used when setting out foundations or frames.

revisionQuestions.q: A load of 2.4 tonnes of sand is delivered. Express this in kilograms.
Explain why over-ordering material is a problem, even though it avoids the risk of running out.
revisionQuestions.a: Over-ordering wastes money on unnecessary material, and the leftover material still has to be stored, returned or disposed of — creating extra cost, handling and environmental waste. Accurate estimation with only a reasonable tolerance for cutting waste is more resource-efficient than ordering a large surplus "just in case".

revisionQuestions.q: A worker records a measurement in chalk directly on the slab instead of on the job card. Is this an acceptable way to record and communicate a measurement? Explain.
revisionQuestions.a: Yes, in the right context — ground spray/chalk marking is a recognised way to record measurements directly on-site (e.g. marking out a layout). However, it should still be confirmed and checked against the drawings/specifications, and for anything that needs to be communicated to others later or kept as a permanent record, a written or digital record (work plan, job card, sketch) is more appropriate since on-site marks can be walked over, washed away or built over.
